title: Install a memory module in the right slot, key first
instruction: Install the memory module in slot A2 and press it down until both latches click shut.
context: Seating memory is a routine step in building and repairing PCs and servers. The module's key notch only fits one way round, and it is only installed once it is pressed in square and both latches have snapped shut.
setup: Left and right are the robot's. Positions are in metres from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left; heights are above the table top. Motherboard: an ATX board (305 x 244 mm, 1.6 mm black glass-epoxy PCB with a CPU socket, VRM heatsinks up to 38 mm tall, M.2 heatsinks and expansion slots), lying flat on the table and fixed to it, its long side along x, centred at (0.262, 0.073), so it spans x 0.110 to 0.415 and y -0.049 to 0.195. Its four DDR5 memory slots (black plastic housings, 133 mm long along x, 6.5 mm wide, top 7.8 mm above the table) are centred at x = 0.320 and, from the robot's left, y = 0.010 (A1), 0.000 (A2), -0.010 (B1) and -0.020 (B2). Each slot has a key 6.8 mm from its centre toward +x (away from the robot), and a black plastic latch at each end with a T-shaped press tab on top; all latches start open, tipped 30 degrees outward. Memory module: a DDR5 desktop module (UDIMM), 133.35 x 31.25 mm green PCB 1.27 mm thick with gold contacts along its bottom edge and a grey aluminium heat spreader on both faces (6.6 mm thick over the spreader, top 34.7 mm above the contact edge), 40 g. Its key notch is 6.8 mm from the centre of its contact edge. It stands upright on its contact edge in a holder, its length along y, centred at (0.32, -0.19), with its key notch on the robot's left of centre (toward the board): a quarter turn clockwise, seen from above, puts it the right way round for A2. Holder: grey plastic block 30 x 150 x 6 mm (x by y) centred at (0.32, -0.19), with two 14 mm wide, 5 mm tall walls along y on top leaving a 2 mm groove in which the module's contact edge stands.
scoring: Judged at the end of the episode, after the arms have let go, from a side photo of the slot and a feeler gauge. 0 if a gripper still holds the module (in simulation, a gripper centre within 4.5 cm of the module's middle), or the module is not standing in A2 the right way round: its centre within 1.5 mm of the slot's centre line and centre, within 5 degrees of the orientation that fits the key, upright within 5 degrees, and its contact edge below the slot's top. A reversed module stops on the key above the slot's top and scores 0, as does a module in another slot or off the table. 0.25: standing in A2 the right way round, neither latch shut. 0.5: one or both latches shut (each latch arm within 5 degrees of upright, its hook in the module's notch) but not the full condition. 1.0 (success, held for 1 s): both latches shut, both ends of the contact edge within 0.3 mm of the slot floor (no gap at the slot's top to a 0.3 mm feeler gauge), the module released and at rest (moved less than 1 mm over the last second). Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0.
reset_notes: Press both latch tabs down to open the latches (this lifts the module's ends), pull the module out, and stand it back in the holder's groove with its key notch toward the board. Check that both A2 latches are fully open.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, 240 Hz physics, 20 Hz control. The board is fixed. The slot's contacts are modelled as compliant strips that pinch the module's edge; 45-degree lead-ins over the strips and the end guides, and a 0.3 mm bevel on the module's edge, centre a module set down within about 2 mm and 1 degree. Seating takes about 16 N pushed square, less than a real DDR5 socket (up to about 107 N), so the arms can do it. Each latch is a hinged body with an over-centre spring: it snaps shut when the module's end treads its foot, and pressing its tab tips it open and lifts that end. No electrical contact or damage is simulated.
